slides.headline: Uruguay's Founding Fathers Weren't The Real Authors
slides.body: Thirty-three rebels declared freedom in 1825. A British diplomat in London decided the borders three years later.

slides.headline: Thirty-Three Men Crossed a River
slides.body: April 1825: Juan Antonio Lavalleja led 33 rebels into Brazilian-ruled Banda Oriental, today's Uruguay, to fight for independence.

slides.headline: Then a Foreign Empire Stepped In
slides.body: Three years of war bled Argentina and Brazil dry. Britain's blockade-choked trade forced both sides to accept a mediator: London.

slides.headline: London Wrote the Borders, Not Rebels
slides.body: British envoy Lord Ponsonby brokered the 1828 Treaty of Montevideo, carving Uruguay out to keep the Río de la Plata trade open.

slides.headline: Soldiers Died So Britain Kept Its Trade
slides.body: Thousands fought and died in the Cisplatine War. The peace that ended it protected British merchants, not Uruguayan self-rule.

slides.headline: Was Uruguay Born Free, or Built?
slides.body: Every August 25, Uruguay celebrates independence. Few ask who really decided where the borders — and the profits — would fall.
